source.title: Uncertainty-based competition between prefrontal and dorsolateral striatal systems for behavioral control.

confidence_rationale: Canonical, heavily replicated normative account whose central move is exactly ARC-120's: two controllers both EXIST and both compute a full answer on every trial, yet behavioural authority is allocated to whichever is currently more accurate rather than shared or granted by default. Held below 0.8 because the paper is a normative/computational proposal rather than a direct test, and because its 'competence' is a per-trial uncertainty estimate rather than the accumulated developmental competence ARC-120's sequence describes.
failure_signatures: A design in which every existing controller contributes to the behavioural output in proportion to nothing but its existence (fixed blend, or unconditional veto) reproduces the failure Daw et al. identify: the statistically inefficient controller drags the accurate one whenever their estimates disagree.

If the arbitration signal is a fixed architectural prior rather than a running estimate of each controller's own accuracy, authority stops tracking competence and the account collapses back to an ad hoc gate.

mapping.source_claim_statement: The brain contains multiple behavioural-choice controllers (a prefrontal/model-based and a dorsolateral-striatal/model-free system); because a surfeit of control creates its own choice problem, the systems compete under a Bayesian arbitration principle in which each controller is deployed when its own predictions are least uncertain -- that is, when it should be most accurate.
mapping.ree_translation: This is the general form of ARC-120's 'competence -> authority' step, stated normatively for behavioural control: the mere existence of a computation confers no behavioural authority; authority is allocated by a running estimate of that computation's accuracy. REE's per-event eligibility (ARC-107), map-stability gating (SD-032b), mode gating (MECH-261) and committed-vs-imagined tagging (MECH-094) are, on ARC-120's reading, four domain-specific instantiations of the same allocation rule Daw et al. derive for action selection.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The paper arbitrates between two ACTION-SELECTION controllers on a per-trial basis. ARC-120 additionally covers WRITE authority (memory consolidation, commitment) and asserts a DEVELOPMENTAL ordering across the lifetime of a mechanism; neither is in scope here. Nothing in this paper bears on the second half of ARC-120 -- whether REE's four existing gates are instances of one principle rather than four unrelated gates -- which is an internal architectural question no external paper can settle.
mapping.source_context: Normative reinforcement-learning theory with simulation, framed against rodent and human instrumental-conditioning data (devaluation, overtraining, lesion dissociations).

confidence_components.notes: Very high source quality (canonical, ~decades of downstream replication). Mapping_fidelity weighted heavily as ARC-120 is architectural: the paper's arbitration principle maps cleanly onto the competence->authority step but not onto the developmental-sequence or write-authority parts of the claim. Transfer risk moderate: the principle is domain-general, but its instantiation as per-trial uncertainty is narrower than ARC-120's notion of competence.
